q: Fundamental definition of anemia based on lab values?
a: Decrease in circulating red blood cell (RBC) mass, typically measured by Hemoglobin (Hb), Hematocrit (Hct), or RBC count.

q: Morphologic classification based on Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)?
a: Microcytic (<80 fL), Normocytic (80–100 fL), and Macrocytic (>100 fL).

q: Primary cause of Microcytic Anemia related to heme synthesis?
a: Iron deficiency (most common), Sideroblastic anemia, and Lead poisoning.

q: Primary cause of Microcytic Anemia related to globin synthesis?
a: Thalassemia.

q: Most common cause of Iron Deficiency Anemia in adult males and postmenopausal females?
a: Chronic GI bleeding (must rule out malignancy).

q: Distinctive lab profile of Iron Deficiency Anemia?
a: Low serum iron, high TIBC (Total Iron Binding Capacity), low Ferritin, and high RDW.

q: Classic clinical triad of Plummer-Vinson Syndrome?
a: Iron deficiency anemia, esophageal webs, and atrophic glossitis.

q: Genetic defect in α-Thalassemia?
a: Gene deletion on Chromosome 16.

q: Genetic defect in β-Thalassemia?
a: Point mutations in splice sites or promoter sequences on Chromosome 11.

q: Appearance of RBCs on blood smear in Thalassemia?
a: Target cells and microcytic, hypochromic cells.

q: Bone marrow finding in Sideroblastic Anemia?
a: Ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria encircling the nucleus).

q: Mechanism of Anemia of Chronic Disease (ACD)?
a: Chronic inflammation increases Hepcidin, which sequesters iron in macrophages and inhibits ferroportin.

q: Lab findings in Anemia of Chronic Disease?
a: Low serum iron, low TIBC, and high/normal Ferritin.

q: Primary mechanism of Megaloblastic Anemia?
a: Impaired DNA synthesis leading to delayed nuclear maturation relative to cytoplasm.

q: Key smear finding in Vitamin B12 or Folate deficiency?
a: Hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes) and oval macrocytes.

q: Neurological symptom unique to Vitamin B12 deficiency (not in Folate)?
a: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal columns/lateral corticospinal tracts).

q: Common cause of B12 deficiency involving an autoimmune process?
a: Pernicious Anemia (destruction of gastric parietal cells/Intrinsic Factor).

q: Reticulocyte response in Hemolytic Anemias?
a: Increased Reticulocyte Count (RC), often >3% (corrected).

q: Distinguishing lab feature of Intravascular Hemolysis?
a: Low Haptoglobin, Hemoglobinuria, and Hemosiderinuria.

q: Inheritance pattern and defect in Hereditary Spherocytosis?
a: Autosomal dominant; defect in RBC membrane proteins (Ankyrin, Spectrin, or Band 3).

q: Diagnostic test for Hereditary Spherocytosis?
a: Osmotic Fragility Test or Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test.

q: Precise molecular mutation in Sickle Cell Anemia?
a: Glutamic acid replaced by Valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain.

q: Primary cause of RBC sickling in HbS patients?
a: Deoxygenation (hypoxia), dehydration, or acidosis.

q: Most common cause of osteomyelitis in Sickle Cell patients?
a: Salmonella.

q: Mutation in Hemoglobin C (HbC)?
a: Glutamic acid replaced by Lysine at position 6 of the β-globin chain.

q: Mechanism of Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
a: Acquired PIGA gene mutation leading to loss of GPI anchor and decay-accelerating factor (CD55/59).

q: Classic presentation of PNH?
a: Dark urine in the morning and increased risk of venous thrombosis (e.g., Budd-Chiari syndrome).

q: Enzyme deficiency causing episodic hemolysis after oxidative stress?
a: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

q: Key smear findings in G6PD deficiency?
a: Heinz bodies (denatured Hb) and Bite cells.

q: Differentiation between Warm and Cold Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia?
a:
Warm is IgG-mediated (extravascular); Cold is IgM-mediated (complement-mediated).

White Blood Cell Disorders: Leukemias & Lymphomas

q: Characterization of Acute Leukemia in the bone marrow?
a: >20% blasts in the marrow.

q: Pathognomonic biopsy finding for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)?
a: Auer Rods (peroxidase-positive cytoplasmic inclusions).

q: Cytogenetic translocation associated with Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL)?
a: t(15;17) involving the Retinoic Acid Receptor (RAR).

q: Standard treatment to induce differentiation in APL?
a: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA).

q: Most common pediatric malignancy?
a: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).

q: Marker for Pre-B and Pre-T ALL?
a: TdT (Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase).

q: Common translocation in B-ALL with a better prognosis?
Hallmark lab finding in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)?
a: Absolute lymphocytosis and "Smudge cells" on peripheral smear.

q: Genetic hallmark of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)?
a: Philadelphia Chromosome t(9;22) forming the BCR-ABL fusion gene.

q: Distinguishing CML from a Leukemoid Reaction?
a: CML has low Leukocyte Alkaline Phosphatase (LAP) score and increased basophils.

q: Target of Imatinib therapy?
a: Tyrosine kinase activity of the BCR-ABL protein.

q: Mutation commonly found in Polycythemia Vera and Essential Thrombocythemia?
a: JAK2 V617F mutation.

q: Clinical sign of Polycythemia Vera after a hot shower?
a: Aquagenic pruritus (due to histamine release from increased mast cells).

q: Pathological cell type in Hodgkin Lymphoma?
a: Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells (CD15+ and CD30+).

q: Most common subtype of Hodgkin Lymphoma?
a: Nodular Sclerosis (often presents with a mediastinal mass in young females).

q: Translocation and gene involved in Follicular Lymphoma?
a: t(14;18) involving BCL-2 overexpression (inhibits apoptosis).

q: Translocation and gene involved in Burkitt Lymphoma?
a: t(8;14) involving c-MYC overexpression.

q: Classic histological appearance of Burkitt Lymphoma?
a: "Starry sky" appearance (tingible body macrophages among neoplastic B cells).

q: Lymphoma associated with chronic H. pylori infection?
a: MALToma (Marginal Zone Lymphoma). Plasma Cell & Myeloid Dyscrasias

q: Triad of Multiple Myeloma?
a: Lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, and monoclonal (M) protein spike.

q: Key finding in the urine of Multiple Myeloma patients?
a: Bence-Jones proteins (free light chains).

q: Characteristic RBC arrangement on smear in Multiple Myeloma?
a: Rouleaux formation (stacks of coins due to high serum protein).

q: Definition of MGUS (Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance)?
a: M-spike <3 g/dL, <10% plasma cells in marrow, and no CRAB symptoms.

q: Features of Waldenström Macroglobulinemia?
a:
Monoclonal IgM spike, hyperviscosity syndrome, and no lytic bone lesions.

Hemostasis & Coagulation

q: Primary hemostasis involves which two components?
a: Platelets and the vessel wall.

q: Adhesion molecule for platelets to subendothelial collagen?
a: von Willebrand Factor (vWF) binding to GP Ib.

q: Common drug that irreversibly inhibits Cyclooxygenase (COX-1)?
a: Aspirin.

q: Lab finding that distinguishes Bernard-Soulier from Glanzmann Thrombasthenia?
a: Bernard-Soulier has large platelets and low GP Ib; Glanzmann has low GP IIb/IIIa.

q: Classic clinical presentation of Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP)?
a: Isolated thrombocytopenia following a viral infection, caused by anti-GP IIb/IIIa antibodies.

q: The "Pentad" of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)?
a: Fever, Anemia (MAHA), Thrombocytopenia, Renal failure, and Neurologic symptoms.

q: Enzyme deficiency in TTP?
a: ADAMTS13 (vWF cleaving protease).

q: Most common inherited bleeding disorder?
a: von Willebrand Disease (vWD).

q: Effect of vWD on lab values?
a: Increased Bleeding Time and potentially increased PTT (vWF stabilizes Factor VIII).

q: Deficiency in Hemophilia A?
a: Factor VIII (X-linked recessive).

q: Deficiency in Hemophilia B?
a: Factor IX (X-linked recessive).

q: Definition of Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)?
a: Pathologic activation of the coagulation cascade leading to widespread microthrombi and subsequent consumption of factors/platelets.

q: Sensitive lab marker for DIC?
a: Elevated D-dimer.

q: Most common inherited cause of Hypercoagulability (thrombophilia)?
a: Factor V Leiden (resistance to Protein C cleavage). Myelodysplastic & Others

q: Definition of Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS)?
a: Cytopenias with hypercellular marrow and maturation defects (ineffective hematopoiesis).

q: Bone marrow finding in Primary Myelofibrosis?
a: Extensive collagen fibrosis (Silver stain positive) and "Dry tap" on aspiration.

q: Characteristic RBC shape in Primary Myelofibrosis?
a: Teardrop cells (Dacrocytes).

q: Function of Protein C and S?
a: Inactivate Factors Va and VIIIa (act as anticoagulants).

q: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis is associated with which deficiency?
a: Protein C deficiency.

q: Mechanism of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
a: IgG antibodies against Heparin-Platelet Factor 4 (PF4) complexes.

q: Preferred anticoagulant in HIT?
a: Direct Thrombin Inhibitors (e.g., Argatroban).

q: Origin of the Thymic Cortex?
a: Third Pharyngeal Pouch.

q: Characteristic cell in Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis?
a: Birbeck granules (tennis racket shape on EM).

q: Most common cause of Eosinophilia?
a: Parasitic infections, Allergies, or Asthma (NAACP: Neoplasia, Asthma, Allergy, Collagen vascular disease, Parasites).

q: Significance of a "Left Shift" in a WBC differential?
a: Increased proportion of immature neutrophils (band cells), indicating acute infection or inflammation.

q: Lab finding in Iron Overload (Hemochromatosis)?
a: High Ferritin, high Serum Iron, and high Transferrin Saturation (>45-50%).

q: Effect of Lead Poisoning on RBCs?
a: Basophilic stippling and inhibition of Ferrochelatase/ALA dehydratase.

q: Vitamin required for the synthesis of ALA (heme precursor)?
a: Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine).

q: Primary site of Erythropoietin (EPO) production?
a: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney.

q: Typical MCV in Sideroblastic Anemia?
a: Microcytic (can sometimes be dimorphic).

q: Role of Hepcidin in iron metabolism?
a: It binds to Ferroportin to degrade it, preventing iron export from enterocytes and macrophages.

q: Cause of "Crew-cut" appearance on skull X-ray?
a: Expansion of marrow space due to severe erythroid hyperplasia (e.g., Sickle Cell or Thalassemia).

q: Difference between Lymphoma and Leukemia?
a: Lymphoma arises as a discrete mass in nodes; Leukemia involves lymphoid or myeloid cells in bone marrow and blood.

q: Characteristic finding in infectious mononucleosis (EBV)?
a: Reactive (atypical) CD8+ T cells (Downey cells).

q: Lymph node region first involved in localized Hodgkin Lymphoma?
a: Cervical or mediastinal nodes.

q: Define Myelophthisic Anemia?
a: Displacement of marrow by infiltrating processes (e.g., metastatic cancer, fibrosis).

q: Lab distinction between Folate and B12 deficiency regarding Methylmalonic Acid (MMA)?
a: B12 deficiency has high MMA; Folate deficiency has normal MMA.

q: Common cause of secondary Polycythemia?
a: Hypoxia (lung disease, high altitude) or EPO-secreting tumors (Renal cell carcinoma).

q: Marker for Myeloid differentiation?
a: Myeloperoxidase (MPO).

q: Marker for Megakaryocytic differentiation?
a: CD41 or CD61.

q: Primary lab screening for Lupus Anticoagulant?
a: Prolonged PTT that does not correct with a 1:1 mixing study (inhibitor present).

q: Target of Desmopressin (DDAVP) in vWD?
a: Induces release of vWF from Weibel-Palade bodies of endothelial cells.

q: Clinical feature of Vitamin K deficiency?
a: Bleeding (increased PT and PTT) due to decreased Factors II, VII, IX, X, C, and S.

q: Source of Vitamin K in humans?
a: Dietary green leafy vegetables and bacterial synthesis in the gut.

q: Cause of Splenomegaly in Pyruvate Kinase deficiency?
a: Work hypertrophy from removing damaged RBCs (extravascular hemolysis).

q: Expected lab change in Chronic Blood Loss?
a: Development of Iron Deficiency Anemia.

q: Major risk of untreated Polycythemia Vera?
a: Hyperviscosity leading to thrombosis (stroke, MI).

q: Defining feature of "Blast Crisis" in CML?
a: Progression of CML to Acute Leukemia (AML or ALL).

q: Key diagnostic marker for Hairy Cell Leukemia?
a: TRAP positive (Tartrate-Resistant Acid Phosphatase).

q: Treatment for Hairy Cell Leukemia?
a: Cladribine (2-CDA).

q: Common location for Extranodal Marginal Zone Lymphoma?
a: Salivary glands (Sjögren), Thyroid (Hashimoto), or Stomach (H. pylori).

q: Typical patient profile for Mantle Cell Lymphoma?
a: Older males; presents with late-stage disease/lymphadenopathy.

q: Translocation for Mantle Cell Lymphoma?
a: t(11;14) involving Cyclin D1.

q: Significance of the "B symptoms" in Lymphoma?
a: Fever, night sweats, and weight loss (indicate poorer prognosis).

q: Function of Antithrombin III?
a: Inhibits Thrombin and Factor Xa; potentiated by Heparin.

q: Common cause of Sideroblastic Anemia (acquired)?
a: Alcoholism, Lead poisoning, or Isoniazid (B6 deficiency).

q: Effect of Splenectomy on RBC morphology?
a: Presence of Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants).

q: Mechanism of Schistocyte formation?
a: Shear stress as RBCs pass through fibrin mesh (Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia).

q: Laboratory feature of Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn (Rh incompatibility)?
a: Positive Direct Coombs test on fetal RBCs.

q: Differentiation between HbS trait and disease on Electrophoresis?
a: Trait (HbAS) has <50% HbS; Disease (HbSS) has >90% HbS and no HbA.

q: Relationship between LDH and Hemolysis?
a: LDH is an intracellular enzyme; levels rise significantly during RBC destruction.

q: Clinical significance of Hairy Cell Leukemia "dry tap"?
a: Marrow fibrosis prevents aspiration.

q: Most common presentation of Follicular Lymphoma?
a: Painless "waxing and waning" lymphadenopathy.

q: Role of the Mantle Zone in a lymph node?
a: Area of B cells surrounding the germinal center.

q: Characteristic of Adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma (ATLL)?
a: Associated with HTLV-1; presents with skin lesions and hypercalcemia.

q: Define Myeloid:Erythroid (M:E) ratio?
a: The ratio of myeloid elements to nucleated erythroid elements in the marrow (Normal is ~3:1).

q: Reason for decreased M:E ratio?
a: Erythroid hyperplasia (hemolysis) or myeloid hypoplasia.

q: Common trigger for Aplastic Crisis in Sickle Cell or Spherocytosis?
a: Parvovirus B19 infection (infects erythroid precursors).

q: Definition of Aplastic Anemia?
a: Pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow (fatty infiltration).

q: Common drugs causing Aplastic Anemia?
a: Carbamazepine, Chloramphenicol, Sulfonamides, and Chemotherapy.

q: Morphologic hallmark of Myelodysplastic Syndrome?
a: Pseudo-Pelger-Huët cells (neutrophils with only two nuclear lobes).

q: Key difference between Acute and Chronic Leukemias?
a: Acute = proliferation of blasts (immature); Chronic = proliferation of mature/differentiating cells.

q: Most common cause of death in Multiple Myeloma?
a: Infection (due to loss of humoral immunity/hypogammaglobulinemia).

q: Classic finding in Amyloidosis associated with Multiple Myeloma?
a: Apple-green birefringence under polarized light with Congo Red stain.

q: Common cause of False Positive VDRL/RPR?
a: Antiphospholipid Syndrome (Lupus anticoagulant/Anticardiolipin antibodies).

q: Preferred diagnostic step for suspected Lymphoma?
a: Excisional lymph node biopsy (rather than Fine Needle Aspiration).

q: Composition of Hemoglobin A2?
a: Two alpha and two delta chains (α<sub>2</sub>δ<sub>2</sub>).

q: Dominant hemoglobin type in a patient with β-Thalassemia major?
a: Hemoglobin F (α<sub>2</sub>γ<sub>2</sub>).

q: Reason for "Chipmunk facies" in Thalassemia?
a: Extramedullary hematopoiesis causing expansion of facial bones.

q: Protective benefit of Sickle Cell Trait?
a: Resistance to Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

q: Leading cause of death in adult Sickle Cell patients?
a: Acute Chest Syndrome.

q: Why is Hydroxyurea used in Sickle Cell Anemia?
a: It increases the production of Hemoglobin F, which interferes with the polymerization of HbS.

q: Clinical consequence of Autosplenectomy in Sickle Cell patients?
a:
Increased susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae).

White Cell & Lymphoid Pathology: Advanced

q: Most common translocation in Follicular Lymphoma?
Protein overexpressed in Mantle Cell Lymphoma?
a: Cyclin D1 (promotes G1 to S phase transition).

q: Defining immunophenotype of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)?
a: CD5, CD19, CD20, and CD23 positive.

q: Common transformation of CLL into Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)?
a: Richter Transformation.

q: Classic presentation of Mycosis Fungoides?
a: Skin patches, plaques, or tumors characterized by Pautrier microabscesses.

q: Definition of Sézary Syndrome?
a: Leukemic phase of Mycosis Fungoides with cerebriform nuclei on blood smear.

q: Histological hallmark of Nodular Sclerosis Hodgkin Lymphoma?
a: Lacunar cells (RS cell variants) and collagen bands circumscribing nodules.

q: Lymphoma associated with Sjögren Syndrome?
a:
MALT Lymphoma of the salivary gland.

Myeloproliferative & Myelodysplastic Neoplasms

q: Characteristic finding in the bone marrow of Essential Thrombocythemia?
a: Increased numbers of enlarged, mature megakaryocytes in clusters.

q: Primary cause of death in Myelofibrosis?
a: Infection, hemorrhage, or transformation to AML.

q: Definition of "Dry Tap" on bone marrow aspiration?
a: Inability to aspirate marrow due to fibrosis (Myelofibrosis) or hypercellularity (Hairy Cell Leukemia).

q: Differentiation between Polycythemia Vera and Stress Erythrocytosis (Gaisböck syndrome)?
a:
PV has increased RBC mass; Stress erythrocytosis has decreased plasma volume with normal RBC mass.

Coagulation & Platelet Dynamics

q: Mechanism of Action of Tranexamic Acid?
a: Antifibrinolytic that inhibits the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin.

q: Result of a 1:1 Mixing Study in Factor VIII Deficiency?
a: The PTT corrects to normal (indicates a deficiency, not an inhibitor).

q: Most common site of bleeding in Hemophilia?
a: Hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints).

q: Effect of Uremia (Renal Failure) on platelet function?
a: Qualitative platelet defect (impaired adhesion and aggregation) with normal platelet count.

q: Diagnostic criteria for Antiphospholipid Syndrome?
a: Clinical thrombosis (or pregnancy loss) plus positive Lupus Anticoagulant, Anti-cardiolipin, or Anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies.

q: Mechanism of Aspirin's antiplatelet effect?
a: Irreversible acetylation of COX-1, preventing Thromboxane A2 (TXA<sub>2</sub>) synthesis.

q: Why is PT (INR) used to monitor Warfarin?
a:
Factor VII has the shortest half-life and is the first to decrease under Warfarin therapy.

Specialized Morphological Findings

q: Appearance of RBCs in Lead Poisoning?
a: Basophilic stippling (due to inhibition of pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase).

q: Appearance of RBCs in Liver Disease?
a: Acanthocytes (spur cells) or Target cells.

q: Appearance of RBCs in Uremia?
a: Echinocytes (burr cells).

q: Finding on peripheral smear in Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (MAHA)?
a: Schistocytes (helmet cells).

q: Histology of the "Starry Sky" pattern in Burkitt Lymphoma?
a:
Sheets of small malignant B cells (the "sky") with interspersed pale-stained tingible body macrophages (the "stars").

Additional Clinical Correlations

q: Most common cause of B12 deficiency in the Western world?
a: Pernicious Anemia.

q: Site of iron absorption in the GI tract?
a: Duodenum.

q: Site of Folate absorption in the GI tract?
a: Jejunum.

q: Site of Vitamin B12 absorption in the GI tract?
a: Terminal Ileum (requires Intrinsic Factor).

q: Condition associated with an elevated Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)?
a: Hereditary Spherocytosis.

q: Why are patients with Sickle Cell and Spherocytosis prone to Gallstones?
a: Chronic hemolysis leads to increased bilirubin, forming pigmented (calcium bilirubinate) stones.

q: Primary treatment for Iron Overload (Hemochromatosis)?
a: Therapeutic phlebotomy.

q: Mechanism of Anemia in Myelophthisic process?
a: Space-occupying lesions (like metastatic cancer) replace hematopoietic tissue.

q: The "Doughnut Cell" (Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma)?
a: Hallmarks cells with kidney-shaped nuclei and ALK protein positivity.

q: Major side effect of Heparin therapy?
a: Bleeding and Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT).

q: Reversal agent for Heparin?
a: Protamine Sulfate.

q: Reversal agent for Warfarin (immediate)?
a: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) or Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC).

q: Reversal agent for Warfarin (delayed)?
a: Vitamin K.

q: Significance of hypersegmented neutrophils?
a: Megaloblastic anemia (B12 or Folate deficiency).

q: Primary pathology in Post-Transfusion Purpura?
a: Development of antibodies against platelet antigens (usually HPA-1a) following transfusion.

q: Common causes of non-megaloblastic macrocytic anemia?
a: Alcoholism, liver disease, and Diamond-Blackfan anemia.

q: Clinical features of Diamond-Blackfan Anemia?
a: Rapid-onset anemia in the first year of life, short stature, and craniofacial or thumb anomalies.

q: Difference between Diamond-Blackfan and Fanconi Anemia?
a: Diamond-Blackfan is pure red cell aplasia; Fanconi is a global pancytopenia (DNA repair defect).

q: Characteristic physical exam finding in Fanconi Anemia?
a: Cafe-au-lait spots, short stature, and absent/hypoplastic radii or thumbs.

q: Laboratory finding in Parvovirus B19-induced Aplastic Crisis?
a:
Acute drop in hemoglobin with a reticulocyte count near 0%.

Hemolysis & RBC Enzymes (Advanced)

q: Inheritance of G6PD Deficiency?
a: X-linked recessive.

q: Why is the Direct Coombs test negative in G6PD deficiency?
a: The hemolysis is due to enzyme deficiency and oxidative stress, not autoantibodies.

q: Definition of the "Warm" antibody in AIHA?
a: IgG antibody that reacts at body temperature (37°C); usually causes extravascular hemolysis.

q: Definition of the "Cold" antibody in AIHA?
a: IgM antibody that reacts at low temperatures; often follows Mycoplasma pneumoniae or EBV.

q: Why do Howell-Jolly bodies appear after splenectomy?
a:
The spleen is no longer present to "pit" or remove nuclear remnants from RBCs.

Myeloproliferative Neoplasms (In-depth)

q: Genetic hallmark of Systemic Mastocytosis?
a: KIT D816V mutation.

q: Diagnostic finding in Systemic Mastocytosis?
a: Increased serum tryptase and clusters of spindle-shaped mast cells in the bone marrow.

q: Clinical presentation of Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS)?
a: Recurrent anaphylaxis, flushing, and diarrhea triggered by heat, exercise, or alcohol.

q: Distinguishing feature of Essential Thrombocythemia (ET) vs. Reactive Thrombocytosis?
a:
ET is a clonal malignancy (often JAK2+); Reactive is driven by cytokines (IL-6) in inflammation or iron deficiency.

Coagulation & Transfusion Medicine

q: Major risk of Large-Volume Transfusion?
a: Dilutional coagulopathy and hypocalcemia (due to citrate anticoagulant in blood bags).

q: Leading cause of transfusion-related fatality?
a: Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI).

q: Mechanism of TRALI?
a: Donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies activate recipient neutrophils in the pulmonary vasculature.

q: Difference between TRALI and TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload)?
a: TRALI is non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (normal PCWP); TACO is volume overload (high PCWP).

q: Lab marker used to monitor Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH)?
a: Anti-Factor Xa assay (PT/PTT are usually unreliable for LMWH).

q: Mechanism of Argatroban?
a: Direct Thrombin Inhibitor (DTI).

q: Primary treatment for a patient with Factor VIII Inhibitors (Acquired Hemophilia)?
a:
Bypassing agents like Activated Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (aPCC) or Recombinant Factor VIIa.

Lymphoid Neoplasms & Histiocytosis

q: Immunophenotype of Mantle Cell Lymphoma?
a: CD5+ and Cyclin D1+; CD23 negative (distinguishes it from CLL).

q: Characteristic cell in Rosai-Dorfman Disease?
a: Large histiocytes showing emperipolesis (engulfment of intact lymphocytes).

q: Clinical triad of Hand-Schüller-Christian Disease?
a: Diabetes insipidus, exophthalmos, and lytic bone lesions (a variant of Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis).

q: "Letterer-Siwe Disease" patient demographic?
a: Infants (<2 years old); presents as a skin rash and multi-organ involvement.

q: Most common site for an Extranodal Marginal Zone Lymphoma?
a: The stomach (associated with H. pylori). General Pathology & Lab Signs

q: Significance of a "Dry Tap" in Bone Marrow?
a: Suggests Myelofibrosis, Hairy Cell Leukemia, or metastatic cancer (marrow is too fibrotic or packed to aspirate).

q: Clinical significance of a "Leukemoid Reaction"?
a: Exaggerated WBC elevation (>50,000) due to infection/stress, simulating leukemia but with mature cells.

q: Definition of Pelger-Huët Anomaly?
a: Benign inherited condition where neutrophils have bilobed (pince-nez) nuclei; can be "pseudo" in MDS.

q: Primary metabolic abnormality in Tumor Lysis Syndrome?
a: Hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia.

q: Consequence of splenic congestion (e.g., in portal hypertension)?
a: Hypersplenism leading to sequestration and destruction of all three blood cell lines (pancytopenia).

q: Defining feature of Splenic Infarcts?
a: Wedge-shaped, pale areas of necrosis due to lack of collateral blood flow (common in Sickle Cell or Emboli).

q: Condition associated with Thymic Hyperplasia?
a: Myasthenia Gravis (present in ~65-75% of cases).

q: Definition of a Thymoma?
a:
Neoplasm of thymic epithelial cells (can be associated with Pure Red Cell Aplasia or Myasthenia Gravis).

Advanced Flow Cytometry & Markers

q: Pan-B cell markers used in flow cytometry?
a: CD19, CD20, and CD21.

q: Pan-T cell markers used in flow cytometry?
a: CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7.

q: Surface marker used to identify hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)?
a: CD34.

q: Diagnostic markers for Reed-Sternberg cells?
a: CD15+ and CD30+.

q: Classic immunophenotype for Mantle Cell Lymphoma?
a:
CD5+, CD19+, and Cyclin D1+.

Myeloid Neoplasms & Rare Variations

q: Clinical feature of Chronic Myelomonocytic Leukemia (CMML)?
a: Persistent monocytosis (>1,000/µL) and absence of the Philadelphia chromosome.

q: Morphology of "Faggot cells" in APL?
a: Promyelocytes containing bundles of Auer rods in the cytoplasm.

q: Significance of "Hypersegmentation" in Myelodysplastic Syndrome?
a: It is a sign of dysgranulopoiesis (though more common in Megaloblastic Anemia). Hemostatic Disorders: Rare & Clinical

q: Mechanism of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)?
a: Shiga-like toxin from E. coli O157:H7 damages endothelial cells, leading to microthrombi.

q: Primary clinical difference between HUS and TTP?
a: HUS predominantly involves renal failure and follows diarrhea; TTP involves CNS symptoms and ADAMTS13 deficiency.

q: Result of Ristocetin Cofactor Assay in von Willebrand Disease?
a: Abnormal (vWF is required for Ristocetin-induced platelet agglutination).

q: Effect of Vitamin C deficiency (Scurvy) on blood vessels?
a: Defective collagen cross-linking leads to weakened vessel walls and easy bruising/petechiae.

q: Pathology of Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP)?
a:
IgA immune complex deposition in small vessels, causing palpable purpura and hematuria.

Special Stains & Diagnostics

q: Purpose of the Prussian Blue stain in Hematology?
a: To visualize iron (ferritin/hemosiderin) in macrophages or ring sideroblasts.

q: Purpose of the Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) stain in Leukemia?
a: Positive in some cases of ALL (shows "chunky" positivity).

q: Significance of "Tartrate-Resistant Acid Phosphatase" (TRAP)?
a: Specific marker for Hairy Cell Leukemia.

q: Most accurate way to confirm a diagnosis of Hemoglobinopathy?
a:
High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) or Hemoglobin Electrophoresis.

Red Cell Metabolism & Structure

q: Enzyme responsible for converting Methemoglobin back to Hemoglobin?
a: Cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH-methemoglobin reductase).

q: Clinical presentation of Methemoglobinemia?
a: Cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen and "chocolate-colored" blood.

q: Role of Ankyrin and Spectrin in the RBC?
a: They maintain the biconcave shape and deformability of the red cell membrane.

q: Definition of "Pancytopenia"?
a: Simultaneous decrease in RBCs, WBCs, and Platelets.

q: Most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in a strict vegan?
a: Dietary deficiency (B12 is only found in animal products).

q: Diagnosis for a child with "painless" cervical lymphadenopathy and a "starry sky" biopsy?
a: Burkitt Lymphoma.

q: Most common pediatric cause of Vitamin B12 deficiency?
a: Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome (selective malabsorption of B12 with proteinuria).

q: Primary pathology in Schwachman-Diamond Syndrome?
a: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and neutropenia (ribosomal stress).

q: Defining RBC morphology in Abetalipoproteinemia?
a: Acanthocytes (spur cells).

q: Most common vascular complication of Sickle Cell Trait?
a:
Renal papillary necrosis (presenting as painless hematuria).

Morphological "Red Herrings" & Artifacts

q: Cause of "Pappenheimer bodies" on a smear?
a: Sideroblastic anemia (these are iron inclusions).

q: Significance of "Cabot rings"?
a: Remnants of mitotic spindles; seen in megaloblastic anemia or lead poisoning.

q: Distinguishing feature of "Pseudo-thrombocytopenia"?
a: Platelet clumping in the presence of EDTA; corrected by using a sodium citrate tube.

q: Cause of "Stomatocytes" (mouth-shaped cells)?
a:
Alcoholism or hereditary stomatocytosis.

Advanced Pharmacology & Therapeutics

q: Mechanism of Eculizumab in PNH?
a: Monoclonal antibody against C5 complement protein (prevents MAC formation).

q: Mechanism of Romiplostim in ITP?
a: Thrombopoietin (TPO) receptor agonist (stimulates platelet production).

q: Primary toxic effect of Doxorubicin in lymphoma treatment?
a: Dilated cardiomyopathy.

q: Mechanism of Cyclophosphamide-induced hemorrhagic cystitis?
a: Accumulation of the metabolite Acrolein in the bladder.

q: Drug used to prevent Hemorrhagic Cystitis?
a:
Mesna.

Systemic Associations

q: Hematologic association with Thymoma?
a: Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) or Good Syndrome (hypogammaglobulinemia).

q: Triad of Felty Syndrome?
a: Rheumatoid Arthritis, Splenomegaly, and Neutropenia.

q: Meaning of "Extramedullary Hematopoiesis"?
a: Blood cell production outside the bone marrow (e.g., liver/spleen), typically due to marrow failure.

q: Finding in the bone marrow of Gaucher Disease?
a: "Crinkled tissue paper" appearance of macrophages (glucocerebrosidase deficiency).

q: Define "Hyperleukocytosis" (Leukostasis)?
a: WBC >100,000; a medical emergency where high blast counts cause vascular occlusion and tissue hypoxia.

q: Diagnostic significance of a "Dry Tap" in an elderly patient with massive splenomegaly?
a: Highly suggestive of Primary Myelofibrosis or Hairy Cell Leukemia.
